fields.definition: A bass drum pedal technique in which a drummer sounds two strokes with one foot in a single rocking motion: the first driven with the heel down (using the heel or ball of the foot), the second by the toe as the heel lifts and the foot rocks forward. It lets a single pedal produce fast double strokes without a double pedal.
fields.plain_english: A way to hit the bass drum twice with one foot in one smooth rock. You play the first note with your heel down. Then you tip forward onto your toes for the second note. It gives you fast doubles from a single pedal.
fields.purpose_function: Enables rapid double strokes and steady fast patterns from one foot and one pedal, improving speed and endurance without adding a second bass drum or a double pedal.
fields.practical_application: Drummers use it for fast bass-drum figures and rolls in rock, metal, and fusion; when miked, each of the two beats should read as an even, separately audible hit.
common_mistakes: Letting the two strokes come out uneven, so the second (toe) note is weak or lost
Tensing the leg and ankle instead of relaxing to let the foot rock, which kills speed and causes fatigue
Burying the beater into the head on both strokes, choking the tone instead of letting it rebound
scenario_contexts: Playing fast double-kick sixteenth notes with only a single pedal
Adding quick bass drum doubles under a groove
An engineer setting a gate so both closely spaced beats trigger cleanly

sources: Vic Firth Education (percussion/drumset technique resources)
DW Drums technical and pedal-technique education resources

fields.definition: A microphone placed inside the cajón, usually reaching in through the rear sound hole, to capture the box's low-frequency body and the rattle of the internal snares. It is commonly paired with an external front mic that captures the slap and attack of the front playing plate (tapa).
fields.plain_english: A mic put inside the cajon box, usually through the round hole in the back. It picks up the deep bass boom and the buzzy snare rattle from inside. Players often add a second mic in front for the sharp slap sound.
fields.purpose_function: Captures the deep bass and internal snare buzz that a front mic misses, giving a fuller and more controllable low end for live reinforcement or recording.
fields.practical_application: A tech clips or tapes a small mic (or uses a cajón with a built-in mic) inside the box, checks polarity against any front mic, and blends the two so bass and slap sit together.
common_mistakes: Combining the inside mic with a front mic without checking polarity, so the low end thins out from phase cancellation
Placing the mic where the player's hand or the internal snares slap it, causing thumps and rattles
Boosting inside-mic low end so much that the sound becomes boomy and undefined
scenario_contexts: Miking a cajón for a singer-songwriter set in a small club
Recording an acoustic session and blending inside and front mics
Using a cajón with a built-in mic plugged into a DI or mixer

sources: Sound on Sound, cajón recording technique
Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques

fields.definition: In darbuka (goblet drum) technique, the 'ka' is a sharp, high-pitched stroke played at the edge of the head with the secondary (usually non-dominant) hand. It produces the same crisp rim tone as a 'tek' but with the other hand, so alternating tek and ka yields fast, even patterns.
fields.plain_english: A short, high tap sound on the darbuka, played at the rim with your weaker hand. It matches the sharp tap your strong hand makes, called a tek. Swapping between the two hands lets you play fast, even rolls.
fields.purpose_function: Gives the drummer an opposite-hand rim stroke so tek-ka alternation can produce quick, smooth runs and fills that one hand alone could not play evenly.
fields.practical_application: A player uses ka as the off-hand fill-in between dum and tek strokes when reading or teaching Middle Eastern rhythms such as maqsum or baladi.
common_mistakes: Striking too far toward the center, so the ka sounds dull instead of sharp and high
Letting the weaker-hand ka come out quieter than the tek, making patterns sound uneven
Confusing ka with dum; ka is a thin rim tone, not the deep center bass
scenario_contexts: Learning the maqsum rhythm where tek and ka alternate
A percussionist filling fast passages by trading tek and ka hands
Notating a darbuka part that marks D, T, and K strokes

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (darabukka / goblet drum)
James Blades, Percussion Instruments and Their History

fields.definition: The buzzing or rattling timbre added to the sustained tone of a plucked lamellophone tine. On traditional African instruments (mbira, likembe) it is produced deliberately with attached shells, bottle caps, beads, or a mirliton sleeve and is musically prized; on modern melodic kalimbas an unintended buzz can also arise from a loose tine, debris, or a tine vibrating against its bridge.
fields.plain_english: A rattly, buzzing sound layered onto a kalimba or mbira note. On many African instruments this buzz is added on purpose with beads, shells, or bottle caps, and it is wanted. On a modern kalimba, a buzz can also be a fault from a loose or dirty key.
fields.purpose_function: Adds a shimmering, sustaining buzz that thickens each note and helps it carry; traditionally it also holds cultural and ritual meaning, while an unwanted buzz signals a setup problem to fix.
fields.practical_application: A player adds or removes buzzers (rings, beads, shells) to taste, while a tech traces an unwanted buzz by reseating the tine, cleaning under it, or adjusting where it clamps.
common_mistakes: Assuming every buzz is a fault; on the mbira and many kalimbas the buzz is added deliberately and desired
Bending or forcing a tine to silence a buzz, which pushes the note out of tune
Ignoring debris or a loose tine base, so an unwanted rattle keeps returning
scenario_contexts: Adding a buzzer ring to a tine for more sustain and shimmer
A traditional mbira with bottle caps producing its characteristic buzz
Troubleshooting a new kalimba that rattles on one note

sources: James Blades, Percussion Instruments and Their History (lamellophones and buzzing devices)
Grove Dictionary of Music (mbira)
Paul Berliner, The Soul of Mbira

fields.definition: The sharp, high-frequency attack of a bass (kick) drum produced by the beater striking the batter head, dominated by energy roughly in the 2-5 kHz range. Engineers emphasize it so the kick's beater 'click' cuts through a dense mix, especially in rock and metal.
fields.plain_english: The short, clicky tick you hear when the kick drum beater hits the head. It lives in the higher frequencies, around a few kHz. Engineers boost it so the kick stays clear even in a loud, busy mix.
fields.purpose_function: Gives the kick definition and attack so each hit is clearly heard through guitars, bass, and cymbals, and so reinforced kicks translate on small speakers.
fields.practical_application: A mixer boosts around 2-5 kHz, uses a harder or plastic beater, adds a patch to the head, or blends a sample to bring out the click when the kick is getting lost.
common_mistakes: Boosting click so hard the kick sounds thin and clicky with no weight behind it
Confusing click (beater attack, high frequencies) with thump (body, low frequencies)
Chasing click with EQ when the real fix is a harder beater or a patch on the head
scenario_contexts: Cutting a metal kick through a wall of distorted guitars
Adding click so the kick shows up on phone and laptop speakers
Blending a click-heavy sample under a soft acoustic kick

sources: Sound on Sound, kick drum recording and mixing
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques

fields.definition: The deep, low-frequency body and weight of a bass (kick) drum, centered roughly in the 50-100 Hz region around its fundamental. It provides the felt 'thump' and power of the kick, as distinct from the higher-frequency beater 'click.'
fields.plain_english: The deep, punchy low end of the kick drum that you feel in your chest. It sits down around 50 to 100 Hz. This is the thump part, separate from the higher clicky attack.
fields.purpose_function: Delivers the low-end power and rhythmic foundation of a track, giving the kick its size and weight in a mix or through a PA.
fields.practical_application: An engineer shapes thump with EQ around 50-100 Hz and by controlling resonance and decay, balancing it against the bass guitar so the low end stays tight, not muddy.
common_mistakes: Piling on low end until the kick booms and masks the bass guitar
Confusing thump (low-frequency body) with click (high-frequency attack)
Boosting thump on speakers that cannot reproduce it, so the change is inaudible and only wastes headroom
scenario_contexts: Tuning kick low end so it locks with the bass guitar
Dialing chest-thump for a live PA with subwoofers
Taming an overly boomy kick in a small room

sources: Sound on Sound, kick drum recording and mixing
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques

fields.definition: The relative firmness of a percussion mallet's head, ranging from soft yarn or cord through medium rubber to hard plastic, acrylic, or brass, which sets how it excites a bar or drum. Harder heads have shorter contact time and excite more high partials for a brighter, more articulate attack; softer heads emphasize the fundamental for a rounder, darker tone.
fields.plain_english: How hard or soft the head of a percussion mallet is, from soft yarn to hard plastic. A hard mallet gives a bright, sharp sound with lots of attack. A soft mallet gives a warm, round tone that brings out the low notes.
fields.purpose_function: Lets a player match tone, attack, and volume to the instrument, register, and music, since the same bar can sound bright or mellow depending on the mallet.
fields.practical_application: A percussionist picks harder mallets for xylophone, the high register, or bright loud passages, and softer mallets for marimba, the low bars, or warm blended playing.
common_mistakes: Using very hard mallets on the low marimba bars, which sounds harsh and can crack the bars
Assuming harder always means louder; past a point it just adds click and noise, not musical volume
Ignoring how hardness must change across the range, so low bars sound weak or high bars sound harsh
scenario_contexts: Choosing yarn mallets for a warm marimba solo
Switching to hard plastic mallets for a bright, cutting xylophone part
Selecting graded mallet sets so each register speaks evenly

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Thomas Rossing, Science of Percussion Instruments

fields.definition: The tuned tubes (traditionally gourds or wood, now usually aluminum) suspended below each marimba bar, each acting as a closed pipe whose air column is tuned to the bar's fundamental frequency (about a quarter wavelength). When the bar vibrates, the matched resonator reinforces the fundamental, making the note louder and fuller while shortening its decay.
fields.plain_english: The tubes hanging under each marimba bar. Each tube is tuned so the air inside rings at the same pitch as the bar above it. This makes each note louder and richer, though it also fades a bit faster.
fields.purpose_function: Amplify and enrich each bar's fundamental so the marimba projects with a full, warm tone rather than the thin, quiet sound of an unmounted bar.
fields.practical_application: A tech keeps resonators aligned and dent-free and may adjust tuning stops or end caps to compensate for temperature and humidity so notes stay at full resonance.
common_mistakes: Thinking resonators change a note's pitch; they reinforce the bar's fundamental, they do not tune the bar
Denting, clogging, or misaligning tubes, which weakens resonance and volume
Ignoring temperature and humidity, so bars and resonators drift out of match and lose fullness
scenario_contexts: Setting up a marimba and aligning bars over their resonators
Adjusting resonator tuning stops for a hot, humid venue
Explaining why an unmounted bar sounds thin without its tube

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Thomas Rossing, Science of Percussion Instruments

fields.definition: The basic, steady bongó pattern of Cuban son and salsa, whose name means 'hammer.' It is a continuous eighth-note ostinato played with fingers and thumbs across the two bongo drums (macho and hembra), anchoring the groove while the player also adds improvised fills.
fields.plain_english: The main hammer pattern a bongo player keeps going in salsa and Cuban son. It is a steady stream of even notes played across the two little drums. It holds the groove while the player throws in extra fills on top.
fields.purpose_function: Provides a constant timekeeping pulse and rhythmic anchor for the ensemble, tying the percussion section to the clave and the rest of the band.
fields.practical_application: A bongocero plays martillo through the verse/son sections, breaks from it for fills, and typically switches to the bell (cencerro) in the montuno.
common_mistakes: Rushing or letting the eighth notes get uneven, so the martillo loses its steady drive
Playing it too loud or too busy so it fights the clave and the rest of the rhythm section
Never leaving the pattern; martillo should breathe with occasional fills, not run mechanically nonstop
scenario_contexts: Holding the groove during the verses of a salsa tune
A bongo player switching from martillo to the bell at the montuno
Teaching a beginner the basic bongo timekeeping pattern

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (bongos)
Ed Uribe, The Essence of Afro-Cuban Percussion and Drum Set
Rebeca Mauleón, Salsa Guidebook
